name: China Manufacturing Scale
narrative: China captured over 80% of global humanoid robot installations in 2025 (~16,000 units worldwide). Unitree shipped 5,500+ units and targets 20,000 in 2026; UBTECH became the first company globally to deliver more than 1,000 industrial humanoids and is targeting 5,000 in 2026 and 10,000 in 2027. US firms lead on AI software and capital raised, but commercial deployment volume remains 10–50× behind. The gap is now the central policy question.

name: Robotics Foundation Models
narrative: The bet that one large model can drive many robot bodies is now well-funded: Skild AI raised $1.4B at a $14B+ valuation in January 2026; Physical Intelligence open-sourced its π0 weights and by late 2025 had raised ~$1.5B total (a $600M Series B at a $5.6B valuation, with talks of an $11B+ round). The unresolved question is whether the right architecture is closed-source-and-vertically-integrated (Figure, Tesla, Apptronik building model + body) or open-source-and-horizontal (Physical Intelligence). Outcome shapes the next decade of robotics IP.

name: Humanoid Cost Trajectory
narrative: 1X opened consumer preorders for NEO at $20,000 in April 2026 — the first humanoid priced for households. China's Unitree priced its G1 at $16,000, putting downward pressure on the research-tier segment. Tesla has publicly targeted sub-$30,000 for Optimus. Industrial humanoids remain materially more expensive: Agility's Digit is reported to cost upwards of $250,000 per unit in commercial deployments. The watch-this-space question: when do US-built industrial humanoids match Chinese unit-economics, and what does the cost curve look like at 10× volume?

name: Defense Robotics Procurement
narrative: DoD Replicator initiative committed $1B to fielding thousands of attritable autonomous systems within 18–24 months. Anduril ($14B valuation) and Shield AI ($5.3B) are the marquee non-traditional primes; both raised heavily on Replicator tailwinds. HR 8189 (American Security Robotics Act) would further restrict federal procurement of foreign-made humanoids. The defense channel is now the most reliable revenue line for robotics startups outside warehouse automation.

name: Federal Policy Momentum
narrative: After years of dispersed activity, 2026 brought concentrated movement: HR 7334 (National Commission on Robotics) and HR 8189 (American Security Robotics Act) introduced in the 119th Congress; the One Big Beautiful Bill Act includes 100% bonus depreciation favoring automation capex; Robots For America launched May 11, 2026 as the industry's coordinated coalition. The watch list for the next six months: whether HR 7334 advances out of committee, OBBB final passage with depreciation provisions intact, and Replicator Tranche 2 size.

name: Physical AI ("AI with a body")
narrative: Physical AI — AI systems that perceive, reason about and act on the material world — became the dominant venture framing of 2026. Eclipse Ventures raised a dedicated $1.3B physical-AI fund (Apr 2026), and a16z, Lux, CapitalG, NVIDIA and SoftBank are all backing the category. Two layers are forming: (1) horizontal robot foundation-model labs (Physical Intelligence, Skild, Field AI, Generalist, Dyna) selling a "brain" that runs across many bodies, and (2) vertical players embedding embodied AI into specific machines — driving (Wayve), construction (Bedrock), delivery (Serve). The open question mirrors the foundation-models debate: does the value accrue to the model, the body, or the deployment?

name: US Robot Component Supply Chain
narrative: China dominates the upstream supply chain for robotics hardware: precision cycloidal and harmonic gear reducers, brushless servo motors, force-torque sensors, and lithium battery packs. US and European humanoid makers source most of these critical components from Chinese or Japanese suppliers. NDAA Section 889 restrictions and tariff escalations are forcing the question: can the US build domestic actuator and motor capacity fast enough to matter? Westmag emerged in 2025 as the first VC-backed US startup explicitly targeting NDAA-compliant drone motors and robot actuators. Hebi Robotics has supplied modular actuators to research institutions for a decade. Moog Inc. (NYSE: MOG.A) remains the largest US precision-actuator manufacturer for defense and aerospace. The policy bet: whether Buy-American mandates, Section 232 tariffs on motors, and manufacturing-capex incentives can seed a domestic supply base before humanoid production scales past one million units per year.
